texts.preamble: Dasari Yadamma vs The State Of Telangana And 2 Others on 26 June, 2023 Author: K. Lakshman Bench: K.Lakshman, P.Sree Sudha Hon'Ble Sri Justice K. Lakshman And Hon'Ble Smt. Justice P. Sree Sudha Writ Petition No.7808 Of 2023 Order:
texts.facts: 2. This writ petition is filed to issue a writ of Habeas Corpus directing respondent No.3 to produce the detenu i.e., Dasari Surender @ Suri @ Moin @ Muneer now detained in Central Prison, Cherlapally, Medchal - Malkajgiri District, and [LEAKAGE_MASK] the impugned detention order passed by respondent No.2 vide proceedings No.205/PD-CELL/CCRB/RCKD/2022, dated 19.12.2022 and the consequential order, if any, passed by respondent No.1. 3. Perusal of impugned order of detention dated 19.12.2022 passed by respondent No.2 would reveal that in between 2008 and 2021, the detenu was involved as many as thirty eight (38) criminal KL,J & PSS,J cases for the offences punishable under the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short 'IPC') and the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (for short 'POCSO Act') within the limits of Rachakonda, Cyberabad and Hyderabad City Commissionerates. Therefore, with a view to prevent him from indulging in such criminal activities in the years 2015 and 2017, an order of detention under the provisions of the Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities of Boot-leggers, Dacoits, Drug-Offenders, Goondas, Immoral Traffic Offenders Land- Grabbers, Spurious Seed Offenders, Insecticide Offenders, Fertiliser Offenders, Food Adulteration Offenders, Fake Document Offenders, Scheduled Commodities Offenders, Forest Offenders, Gaming Offenders, Sexual Offenders, Explosive Substances Offenders, Arms Offenders, Cyber Crime Offenders and White Collar or Financial Offenders Act, 1986 (for short 'Act, 1986') was made against him by the Commissioner of Police, Hyderabad City vide proceedings 1) No.SB (1) No.56/PD/S1/ 2015, dated 16.12.2015; 2) No.S.B. (1) No.234/PD/S1/2017, dated 27.10.2017 and detained him in Central Prison, Chenchalguda. In the year 2018, the detenu filed a writ petition vide W.P. No.12738 of 2018 and the same was dismissed on 03.07.2018. KL,J & PSS,J Dasari Yadamma vs The State Of Telangana And 2 Others on 26 June, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/39187026/ 1 4. The impugned order dated 19.12.2022 is passed by the Detaining Authority relying on two Crimes registered against the detenu i.e., (i) Crime No.1449 of 2022 registered by the Police, L.B. Nagar Police Station, for the offences punishable under Sections - 302, 498A, 201 and 120B r/w 109 and 34 of IPC; and (ii) Crime No.622 of 2022 registered by the Police, Chaitanyapuri Police Station for the offence punishable under Section - 324 of IPC. 5. The allegations levelled against the detenu in Crime No.1449 of 2022 are that the detenu grew wild on his wife suspecting her fidelity and beat her indiscriminately with a deadly weapon constantly resulting her instant death on 30.08.2022. In the said crime, first bail application filed by him was dismissed. Whereas, the allegations levelled against the detenu in Crime No.622 of 2022 are that the complainant therein and the detenu were known to each other, and out of such acquaintance, the detenu took hand loan on many occasions but did not repay the same. While so, on 30.08.2022 at about 18.00 hours, while the complainant was near Chaitanyapuri, the detenu again asked him an amount of Rs.1,000/- on which the complainant asked him to repay the earlier loan amounts upon which, the detenu KL,J & PSS,J picked up an altercation and beat him with a stick on his head and fled away. The investigation in the said crime is pending.
texts.arguments: 6. It is contended by learned counsel for the petitioner that the crimes alleged against the detenu can be dealt with by ordinary law before a Competent Criminal Court instead of passing impugned detention order. There is no nexus between the offences allegedly committed by the detenu warranting respondent No.2 to pass impugned order. Further, the grounds referred to in the detention order are stale and not proximate to the order of detention. Thus, the order of detention under Section - 3 (2) of the Act, 1986 has been passed and approved vide G.O.Rt.No.242, dated 17.02.2023 in a mechanical manner. 7. He would further submit that preventive detention of a person is an extreme measure resorted to by the State when ordinary criminal law is found not adequate to control his activities which cause disturbance to public order. In the case on hand, there is no disturbance caused to public order and it would utmost disturb the maintenance of law and order. Thus, passing of order of detention by KL,J & PSS,J respondent No.2 and the consequential confirmation passed by respondent No.1 is illegal and the same is liable to be [LEAKAGE_MASK]. He has also relied on the decision rendered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Khaja Bilal Ahmed v. State of Telangana1. 8. On the other hand, learned Special Government Pleader appearing on behalf of the respondents would contend that the Detaining Authority having satisfied with the material available on record and considering the nature of offence and the manner in which it was committed by the detenu, passed the order of detention. He would further submit that, earlier, thirty eight (38) crimes were registered against the detenu. The offences committed by the detenu are grave in nature. The Detaining Authority considering that there is every possibility of the detenu committing similar offences in future, which would again certainly affect the public order, issued detention order. There is no error in it. The offence Dasari Yadamma vs The State Of Telangana And 2 Others on 26 June, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/39187026/ 3 alleged in Crime No.622 of 2022 is punishable under Section - 324 of IPC. 14. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Ashok Kumar v. Delhi Administration2 observed that preventive detention is devised to afford protection to society. The object is not to punish a man for having done something but to intercept before he does it and to prevent him from doing. 16. In Ram Manohar Lohia v. State of Bihar3, the Apex Court held as under: "...Does the expression "public order" take in every kind of disorder or only some? The answer to this serves to distinguish "public order" from "law and order" because the latter undoubtedly takes in all of them. Public order if disturbed, must lead to public disorder. Every breach of the peace does not lead to public disorder. When two drunkards quarrel and fight there is disorder but not public disorder. They can be dealt with under the powers to maintain law and order but cannot be detained on the ground that they were disturbing public order. Suppose that the two fighters were of rival communities and one of them tried to raise communal passions. The problem is still one of law and order but it raises the apprehension of public disorder. Other examples can be imagined. The . (1982) 2 SCC 403 . (1966) 1 SCR 709 KL,J & PSS,J contravention of law always affects order but before it can be said to affect public order, it must affect the community or the public at large. A mere disturbance of law and order leading to disorder is thus not necessarily sufficient for action under the Defence of India Act but disturbances which subvert the public order are. A District Magistrate is entitled to take action under Rule 30(1)(b) to prevent subversion of public order but not in aid of maintenance of law and order under ordinary circumstances. It will thus appear that just as "public order" in the rulings of this Court (earlier cited) was said to comprehend disorders of less gravity than those affecting "security of State", "law and order" also comprehends disorders of less gravity than those affecting public order". Law and order represents the largest circle within which is the next circle representing public order and the smallest circle represents security of State. It is then easy to see that an act may affect law and order but not public order just as an act may affect public order but not security of the State." Dasari Yadamma vs The State Of Telangana And 2 Others on 26 June, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/39187026/ 4 17. In Kanu Biswas v. State of W.B.4, the Apex Court relying on Ram Manohar Lohia3 noted that preventive detention can only be (1972) 3 SCC 831 KL,J & PSS,J invoked in cases of breach of public order. The Court explained the difference between law and order and public order by stating that public order is said to be affected when the action of the detenu is in the nature of adversely affecting the even tempo of life of the community which causes a general disturbance of public tranquility.
